title.en: Phrasal verbs: three-word verbs and multiple meanings
title.es: Phrasal verbs: verbos de tres palabras y varios significados

summary.en: At C1 you meet **three-word phrasal verbs** (verb + adverb + preposition) such as _put up with_, _look forward to_, _come up with_ and _run out of_. They are **inseparable**: the object always comes at the end (_I can't put up with the noise_). If the last word is **to**, it is a preposition, so a verb after it takes **-ing**: _I'm looking forward to seeing you._ Many phrasal verbs have several meanings (_pick up_ a parcel, a language or speed), so learn them in context. In a formal email or report, a one-word verb often sounds better (_tolerate_, _devise_, _postpone_), but in Speaking part 4 phrasal verbs make your English sound natural.
summary.es: Los de tres palabras no se separan: *put up with it*, no *put it up with*. Si acaban en **to** (look forward to, get round to), ese to es preposición y lleva -ing: looking forward to seeing, no *to see*.

form: Three-word verbs: **verb + adverb + preposition + object** (_get away with it_, _make up for lost time_)
Never separated: _put up with the noise_, not _put the noise up with_
When the last word is **to**, use **-ing**: _look forward to hearing_, _get round to doing_
Passive of verbs with an object: _The decision was put off._ _The problem was dealt with quickly._
Nouns from phrasal verbs: _breakdown, outcome, setback, check-in, take-off_
Formal equivalents: _carry out_ → perform; _put off_ → postpone; _find out_ → discover; _put up with_ → tolerate; _come up with_ → devise

uses.text: **Dealing with problems** → _We came up with a plan to cut costs. I can't put up with this noise any longer._
**Relationships and attitudes** → _She looks up to her grandmother. He gets on with everyone at work._
**Running out and catching up** → _We've run out of paper. I'll catch up with you at the station._
**Several meanings of one verb** → _pick up_: collect (a parcel), learn (a few words), improve (sales picked up).

note.en: Note the meaning, the structure and whether the verb is separable each time you learn it.
note.es: Anota siempre significado, estructura y si se puede separar.

uses.text: **Ending a formal email** → _I look forward to hearing from you._

note.en: Look forward to hearing from you is correct and useful at the end of the formal email in Writing part 4.
note.es: Look forward to hearing from you es el cierre habitual del correo formal.

mistakes.wrong: I look forward to hear from you.
mistakes.right: I look forward to hearing from you.

why.en: To in look forward to is a preposition, so the verb that follows takes -ing.
why.es: Ese to es preposición: hearing, no hear.

why.en: The preposition of belongs to the verb run out of.
why.es: Run out of: no olvides la preposición.

mistakes.wrong: I can't put up the noise.
mistakes.right: I can't put up with the noise.

why.en: Put up with (tolerate) needs all three words.
why.es: Tolerar es put up with; put up solo no vale.

mistakes.wrong: She came up an excellent idea.
mistakes.right: She came up with an excellent idea.

why.en: Come up with is a three-word verb meaning to think of something.

examples.en: I can't put up with the noise from the building site any longer.
examples.es: No soporto más el ruido de las obras.

examples.en: The team came up with a clever plan to cut costs.
We've run out of paper, so please order some more.
I'm really looking forward to meeting you next week.
examples.es: Tengo muchas ganas de conocerte la semana que viene.

examples.en: He got away with it because nobody had seen him.
She works hard to make up for the time she lost last year.
They look down on people who haven't been to university.
We wanted to buy the house, but the deal fell through at the last minute.
After a slow start, sales picked up in the spring.
I'll try to catch up with you after the meeting.
The company is cutting down on travel to reduce its costs.
I haven't got round to answering your email yet; I'll do it tonight.

practice.prompt: I can't ___ the noise from the building site any longer.
We've ___ paper, so please order some more.

explanation.en: Run out of means to have none left.

practice.prompt: I'm looking forward ___ you at the conference.

explanation.en: To is a preposition here, so the verb takes -ing.

practice.prompt: We wanted to buy the house, but the deal ___ at the last minute.

explanation.en: Fall through means a plan or agreement fails to happen.
